# Centring: what it changes and what it doesn't {.unnumbered}

*First raised in [R5](../regression/r5-moderation.qmd). Optional.*

## What it is

**Centring** a variable means subtracting its mean, so that 0 stands for an average case. In a model with an interaction (X, W and X × W), centring X and W changes some numbers and leaves others exactly as they were.

## Why it happens

In a model with an interaction, the coefficient of X is the effect of X **when W = 0**, and the coefficient of W is the effect of W when X = 0. If 0 is not a meaningful value (stress and support are both scored 1 to 5, so neither can be 0), those coefficients describe an impossible person. Centring moves 0 to the average, so they describe the effect at the average of the other variable. The interaction coefficient, its test and R² do not depend on where 0 is, so they do not change.

## A worked example

Wellbeing on stress, support and their product in the Student Life Survey (N = 520):

| Coefficient | Raw scores | Centred scores |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Stress | −0.85 (SE 0.16) | −0.46 (SE 0.04) |
| Support | −0.12 (SE 0.13) | 0.19 (SE 0.04) |
| Stress × support | 0.103 (SE 0.041) | 0.103 (SE 0.041) |
| R² | .307 | .307 |

With raw scores, support appears to have a small *negative*, non-significant effect: that is its effect for a student with zero stress, who cannot exist. Centred, support has a clear positive effect for a student with average stress. The interaction is identical in both.

## The collinearity myth

Centring is often recommended to "reduce multicollinearity". The correlation between stress and the product term does fall, from .69 with raw scores to .02 after centring. But this collinearity was **non-essential**: it came only from where 0 was, and it never affected the interaction test. Centring makes the lower-order coefficients easier to interpret; it does not fix a statistical problem [@aiken1991].

## Why it matters later

- Choosing where time = 0 in a growth model is the same decision: it changes what the intercept means, not the fit. See the [optional growth topic](../sem/optional-growth.qmd) and its app.
- In multigroup models, the "average" person differs between groups, so say which mean you centred on.
